analysis.one_liner: Requires clearer front-of-package nutrition labels, honest ingredient claims, and full nutrition disclosure for online food sales.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Health Committee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make food companies put a standardized symbol on the front of every package flagging calories, added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat. It would require products marketed as containing whole grains, fruit, or vegetables to say how much they actually contain, define terms like "natural" and "healthy," and require online grocers to show the full label information before you buy. It was introduced by Senator Blumenthal and four Democratic colleagues, referred to the Senate Health Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers trying to make quick decisions at the grocery store, parents of children with food allergies, people with celiac disease or kidney disease who need to track gluten or phosphorus, and the growing share of households that buy groceries online would get clearer, more complete information about what is in their food.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grocery shoppers and people with food allergies

how_it_helps.text: Every packaged food would need a standardized front-of-package symbol showing calories, added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat, designed so shoppers can compare products at a glance without nutrition expertise.

Products marketed with terms like "whole wheat," "fruit," "veggie," or "yogurt" would have to disclose the actual percentage of whole grains or the actual quantity of fruit, vegetable, or yogurt per serving, so a sugary drink with fruit pictures cannot imply it contains real fruit servings.

Food sold online would have to display nutrition facts, ingredients, and allergen information prominently on the first product page before purchase, and platforms could not charge an extra fee for it or hide it behind marketing, with civil penalties up to $1 million for violations.

Labels would have to disclose phosphorus (important for kidney patients), caffeine above 10 mg per serving, sugar alcohols and isolated fibers, and artificial dyes or sweeteners, and the FDA could add new major food allergens by regulation.
The FDA would have to define "natural" and tighten "healthy" claims, require more readable ingredient lists, and post all submitted label information in a public, searchable database on its website.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food manufacturers, who would bear the cost of redesigning labels and reformulating or repositioning products whose marketing claims would no longer hold up, plus online grocery platforms subject to new penalties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Packaged food makers and online grocers

drawbacks.text: Companies would face significant relabeling and compliance costs, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for failing to submit label information and up to $1 million for online-disclosure violations; smaller producers could bear these costs disproportionately.
The main requirements would not take effect until three years after enactment, after a one-year proposed-rule deadline and a two-year final-rule deadline, so benefits would be years away.

Defining terms like "natural" (the bill excludes synthetic ingredients and corn syrup from the definition) would be contested and could trigger litigation and reformulation costs that get passed through to prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit — standardized, at-a-glance nutrition signaling and truthful ingredient claims, online and on the shelf — is real and the mechanisms are concrete. The main cost is compliance and relabeling expense for food companies, some of which would reach consumers through prices, and a long phase-in before any of it takes effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on April 26, 2023, joined by Senators Whitehouse, Markey, Booker, and Cardin.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion House action, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food manufacturers and online grocery platforms are better off, since they avoid the relabeling costs, claim restrictions, and penalty exposure the bill would have imposed. Consumers continue to rely on existing labels, where terms like "natural" remain undefined and fruit-flavored products need not say how much fruit they contain.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Packaged food makers avoiding new label rules

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Food Labeling Modernization Act of 2023 in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it received no action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Packaged food and grocery manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed mandatory front-of-package labeling and stricter definitions of terms like "natural," which would constrain marketing claims and require costly relabeling.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill's death in a Democratic-chaired committee meant it faced no recorded floor vote to break down by party.

industries.note: The bill would force quantified disclosure behind 'whole grain,' 'fruit,' and 'veggie' claims, a front-of-package symbol flagging sugars, sodium, and saturated fat, and penalties for noncompliance — directly constraining how sugary and processed products are marketed. Its defeat leaves current label marketing untouched.

Platforms and sellers of food online would have had to display full nutrition, ingredient, and allergen information free of charge at the point of sale, with civil penalties up to $1 million. Nothing changed.

Drinks marketed to parents of children under three could no longer be called 'formula' and would need honest names like 'sweetened milk-based drink' plus warnings against serving to infants. The bill's death preserves that marketing latitude.
